rough.hint: No FSD yet. List the features or epics, mark each as Application, Data platform or AI product, and give it a T-shirt size and complexity. Data platform and AI product features expand into their own drivers using the proxies under Assumptions. Application features expand into screens, fields, APIs, integrations, rules, journeys, batch and file interfaces, events and workflows. Channels and languages apply to the whole scope.
rough.empty: No features yet. Add one to start the rough estimate.

page.readOnly: You are viewing this estimate. Only Estimators and QE Leads of the project can change it.

detailTab.hint: FSD available. Work through the sections in order and open one to edit it. Each header shows what the section currently adds up to. Data platform and AI product sections only count when the change has those requirements.

app.hint: Count each item in the FSD by complexity. The Complexity guide (section 9) explains how to choose Simple, Medium or Complex.
app.roughCmp: Rough said {f} fields, {r} roles, {a} protected actions, {w} approval workflows, {k} critical rules, {v} variants and {l} languages.

fields.hint: Input fields are the fields users enter on screens. API request fields are the unique fields in request DTOs; response and event payload fields are the unique fields the service returns or publishes. Count shared DTOs once. Take them from the FSD or the OpenAPI spec, or leave 0 to estimate.
fields.response: Response and event payload fields, unique (0 = estimate)
fields.apiNote: Estimated if left at 0: {r} request fields and {p} response and payload fields from {a} APIs and {t} topics, after {u} DTO reuse.
fields.byType: Fields by type (optional, from the FSD field list)
fields.byTypeHint: Leave every count at 0 to use Input fields (total) with the typical field mix under Assumptions. Once you enter any count here, these counts replace the total.
fields.lockedNote: Input fields (total) is now locked to {n}, the sum of the counts above. Set every count back to 0 to type a total again.
fields.mixNote: No counts entered, so the model uses Input fields (total), {n}, with the typical field mix: {p} matrix cases per field.

rules.hint: Protected actions are permission-checked actions outside workflows, such as view balance or export; role-gated workflow transitions are added automatically. Critical rules are regulatory or money-moving rules such as AML thresholds, limits, interest and fees. Variants are the products, customer segments or currencies that change a rule's outcome.

data.hint: Fill this section when the change has Data Lake, Data Warehouse or ETL requirements; leave it at 0 otherwise. Counts come from the source-to-target mapping spec, the data model and the data quality catalogue.

ai.hint: Fill this section when the change has chatbot, OCR or AI workflow requirements; leave it at 0 otherwise. AI outputs are not deterministic, so they are sized as labelled evaluation samples, human review per run and analysis, not as pass/fail cases. Golden sets, prompts and OCR samples must be synthetic or anonymised: never real customer data, citizen ID scans or statements.

pt.hint: List the business journeys, APIs, batch jobs and AI calls that must meet performance targets. Performance testing is sized by scripted scenarios, test runs and test-and-tune cycles, not by test cases, and is included in the combined QE total.
pt.scen: Performance scenarios (journeys or APIs under load)
pt.note: Test types apply to rough and detailed mode. Simple: one API. Medium: a short journey or batch job. Complex: a multi-step journey with login, correlation and dynamic data, or an AI call under load.

derived.hint: Calculated from the counts above, the assumptions and the shift-left evidence. Each row matches a driver row in the rough vs detailed comparison.

f.rule: ({k} critical × full table + {s} standard × {std}) × variants {v}× × mutation {m}×
f.fieldTyped: {f} fields by type × {p} matrix cases each × {s} back in SIT
f.fieldMix: {f} fields × {p} matrix cases each (typical mix) × {s} back in SIT
f.fieldBE: ({f} request fields, {src}, × {p} matrix cases + {a} APIs × {o} API-only cases) × {s} back in SIT
f.mapping: {f} response and payload fields, {src}, × {m} × (1 + {fs} format checks) × {s} back in SIT
f.channel: screen and journey cases × {w} (second web stack) + screen cases × ({l} − 1) × {ls}
f.mobile: {n} mobile channel(s): (web journey cases × share + (web screen cases × share + screens × share × mobile-only cases) × (1 + {d} devices)){up} + {r} release cases
f.dataSource: {n} feeds × {c} cases by complexity × {s} (data contract credit)
f.dataModel: {n} tables × {c} cases by complexity + {d} SCD dimensions × {e}
f.dataMapping: {n} mapped columns × {c} checks × {s} back in SIT
f.dataQuality: {n} data quality rules × {c} cases × {s} back in SIT
f.dataPrep: {n} feeds × {h} h × {c} load cycles (hours, no cases)
f.aiIntent: {n} intents × {u} utterances by complexity × {l} languages; label {m} min, review {r} of outputs × {i} runs
f.aiRag: {n} sources × {q} questions × {l} languages; reference answer {m} min
f.aiOcr: {n} document types × {q} samples by complexity; label {m} min each
f.aiEval: {i} evaluation runs × {h} h analysis (hours, no cases)
f.ptDesign: {n} scenarios × {s} h scripting by complexity × (1 − {r} reused) + workload model {w} h + test data {d} h = {h} h
f.ptRun: {n} runs, {r} h per cycle × {c} cycles × (1 + {a} analysis) + {p} h report = {h} h

guide.hint: How to choose Simple, Medium or Complex. Hours per item use the detailed-mode effort settings, before shift-left credits, uplifts and variants.

api.0: Read or basic CRUD, few fields, no downstream call
api.1: Business logic, one downstream call or a state change
api.2: Orchestrates several systems, moves money, or has compensation or rollback paths

screen.0: Display or a simple form with fewer than 10 fields
screen.1: Form with conditional fields, lookups or several actions
screen.2: Multi-step wizard, dynamic sections or complex page state

integration.0: One-way call to a stable system that has a sandbox
integration.1: Request and response with mapping and error codes
integration.2: Asynchronous or two-way, retries, reconciliation, or a core-banking system with test windows

rule.0: One or two conditions, one outcome
rule.1: Three or four conditions, or a tiered value
rule.2: Five or more conditions, several outcomes, or dates and thresholds combined

workflow.1: 4 to 6 transitions with a reject or rework path
workflow.2: 7 or more transitions, parallel approvals, timeouts or escalation

batch.0: One file or job with no dependencies
batch.1: Depends on another job, or has rejects to handle
batch.2: Chain of jobs with cut-off, restart and reconciliation

event.1: Consumer updates state and must ignore duplicates
event.2: Ordering matters, saga or compensation, replay

journey.2: Four or more systems, or money moving end to end

feed.label: Data source or feed
feed.0: One file or table, stable schema
feed.1: Several entities or CDC, occasional schema change
feed.2: Many entities, late or out-of-order data, frequent schema change

pipe.label: ETL / ELT pipeline
pipe.2: Many sources, SCD history, incremental logic and dependencies

table.label: Target table
table.1: Cleansed table with keys and rules
table.2: Curated fact or dimension with history

report.label: Report, mart or dashboard
report.2: Regulatory or financial totals reconciled to source

intent.label: Chatbot intent
intent.1: Several turns or slots, one tool call
intent.2: Multi-step task with tools, authorization and hand-off

ocr.label: OCR document type
ocr.2: Handwriting, stamps, poor scans or many versions

groups.spares: What each L1 test spares SIT

mut.desc: Measures the domain and service unit tests (JUnit 5 + Mockito): do they fail when the logic is wrong?

rule.desc: Share of business rules with decision-table unit tests (limits, fees, eligibility, rate-limit buckets)

be.desc: Jakarta constraints on request DTOs, entities and custom annotations, each with a failing test

map.desc: MapStruct or ModelMapper mappers and @JsonTest: field names, money, dates, enums, nulls, hidden internal fields

jacoco.desc: Shows which code the unit tests ran

fe.desc: Validators and Zod schemas that mirror the backend constraints (field validation matrix)

feunit.desc: Vitest or Jest on pure TypeScript, pipes, signal stores, hooks, reducers and selectors

femut.desc: Checks that the frontend unit tests fail when UI logic is wrong

ios.desc: Coverage of view models, services and validators in the Swift app

android.desc: Coverage of view models, repositories and validators in the Kotlin app

dq.what: Data pipeline tests (dbt tests, Great Expectations)
dq.desc: Share of mapped columns and data quality rules tested in CI

contract.desc: Share of source feeds with schema or contract tests in CI

evalci.desc: The golden set is re-scored on every model, prompt or retrieval change

reuse.desc: Share of AI evaluation samples already labelled in an earlier release

ptci.desc: k6 or Gatling runs per service in Jenkins with latency budgets

apm.desc: Traces, metrics and dashboards already available in the performance environment

ptreuse.desc: Share of scenarios scripted in an earlier release

l4.desc: Cross-system journeys run by QE in SIT

eff.mutOk: Business-rule cases and retest rate stay at base.
eff.mutWeak: Business-rule cases +{u}%, retest rate {w}% instead of {r}%.
eff.creditApi: SIT runs {n} sample case per API.
eff.creditScreen: SIT runs {n} sample case per screen.
eff.creditPartial: {p}% of field cases come back into SIT.
eff.creditFull: SIT repeats the full field-type matrix by hand: about {n} cases per field.
eff.l4On: {n} journey cases in the detailed estimate.
eff.l4Off: Journeys are excluded from SIT sizing.
eff.mapOk: SIT does not re-check field mapping or JSON formats.
eff.mapPartial: {p}% of mapping checks come back into SIT: {n} cases.
eff.mapFull: SIT checks every API response and event payload by hand: {n} cases.
eff.jacoco: Informational, not credited. Coverage shows the code ran; the mutation score shows the tests catch bugs, so only mutation changes the estimate.
eff.feunitWeak: Screen cases +{u}%: UI logic defects reach SIT.
eff.femutWeak: Screen cases +{u}%: weak frontend tests let defects through.
eff.ruleOk: Standard rules: SIT runs {n} wiring case per rule. Critical rules are always tested in full.
eff.rulePartial: {p}% of standard-rule cases come back into SIT. Critical rules are always tested in full.
eff.ruleFull: SIT runs every decision-table case for every rule.
eff.mobileOff: Select the channel in the scope tabs to count it.
eff.ptOff: Mark features as performance-critical or add scenarios to count it.
eff.ptciOn: {c} test and tune cycles instead of {d}.
eff.ptReuseOn: Scripting effort falls by the same share.
eff.ptReuseOff: Every scenario is scripted from scratch.
eff.daOff: Add data platform or AI product drivers in the scope tabs to count it.
eff.dqSample: SIT repeats {s} of column and data quality checks as a sample.
eff.dqPartial: {s} of column and data quality checks come back into SIT.
eff.dqFull: SIT checks every mapped column and data quality rule.
eff.ctSample: SIT runs one check per feed.
eff.ctPartial: {s} of feed cases come back into SIT.
eff.evalci: A person reviews {p} of outputs per evaluation run.
eff.reuseOff: Every sample is labelled from scratch.

r0.test: Domain and service unit tests (JUnit 5 + Mockito)
r0.proves: Method logic, calculations, business rules and error paths of one class, with its collaborators mocked
r0.effect: Below the gate: business-rule cases +25% and retest rate 30% instead of 20%

r1.proves: That the unit tests fail when the code is wrong, which line coverage alone cannot show
r1.measured: Score ≥ 70% overall, 80% in service and domain packages
r1.effect: Drives the business-rule and retest effect above

r2.proves: Every Jakarta constraint on DTOs, entities and custom annotations rejects bad input
r2.effect: Credits backend field cases: one sample per API, half, or all of them

r3.proves: Entity, DTO and JSON stay in step: names, money, dates, enums and nulls map correctly and internal fields stay hidden
r3.measured: Share of mappers and DTOs with tests
r3.effect: Credits about 1.4 checks per response or payload field

r4.test: Business rule unit tests (limits, fees, eligibility, rate-limit buckets)
r4.proves: Every decision-table branch and threshold of a rule, without Spring
r4.measured: Share of rules with decision-table unit tests; PIT checks their strength
r4.effect: Credits standard rules: one wiring case each, half, or the full table. Critical rules always run in full

r5.proves: Which code ran during the tests
r5.effect: Informational only, so the same tests are not credited twice

r6.proves: The UI rejects what the API rejects, field by field
r6.effect: Credits frontend field cases: one sample per screen, half, or all of them

r7.proves: Pure TypeScript logic, pipes, signal stores, hooks, reducers and selectors

r8.test: iOS and Android unit tests (XCTest, JUnit, Espresso)
r8.proves: View models, services, repositories and validators of the native apps
r8.effect: Below the gate: that platform's mobile cases +20%

r9.proves: That the frontend unit tests fail when UI logic is wrong

evidenceTab.footnote: L2 slices, L3 integration and L4 contract tests also shift work left, but this tab credits only L1 evidence. Their effect shows up in fewer defects and a lower retest rate once you calibrate.

teamTab.mixNorm: Mix adds up to {n}%. The model normalises it to 100%.
teamTab.autoOn: {a}% of the regression pass is automated, so manual regression covers {m}% of cases instead of {r}%.
teamTab.autoOff: The regression pass is fully manual.
teamTab.aiOn: {lvl}: test design time −{p}%, including validation design. Use only synthetic data in prompts and generated test data, never real customer data or PII.
teamTab.aiOff: No AI assistance assumed. Turn it on only after a pilot has measured the saving on your own work.
teamTab.calDataOver: Data: {c} load cycles × {d} days = {n} days, longer than the {w}-day SIT window. Plan extra batch runs or a longer window.
teamTab.calDataFits: Data: {c} load cycles × {d} days = {n} days fits the {w}-day SIT window.
teamTab.calAi: AI: the golden set needs about {h} SME labelling hours: {d} working days with {s} SMEs.
teamTab.calAiOver: That is more than half the window ({w} days); start labelling before SIT or add SMEs.
teamTab.calAiFits: It fits in the first half of the window, before evaluation runs start.
teamTab.calPt: Performance: {c} test and tune cycles × {d} days = {n} days in a production-like environment, with fixes between cycles. Book the environment slot early; soak runs often need nights or weekends.
teamTab.calPtOver: This is longer than the SIT window; start performance testing earlier.
teamTab.calNone: No data platform, AI product or performance scope in this estimate, so there is nothing to check.
teamTab.hpf: Hours one FTE can give in the window
teamTab.blend: Blended capacity factor for this mix

trace.title: Worked example: how the current detailed estimate is built
trace.hint: This trace updates as you change inputs. Follow it from scope to FTE to check the arithmetic.
trace.scope: Scope: {a} APIs, {s} screens, {i} integrations, {r} rules, {w} workflows, {b} batch jobs, {e} event topics, {j} journeys on {ch}.
trace.cases: Cases: counted drivers × cases per driver by complexity, plus the derived rows (validation, mapping, roles, mobile, accessibility), after shift-left credit = {n} cases and samples.
trace.appHours: Application hours: each case gets {d} design minutes plus its execution minutes × (cycles {cy} + regression {rg} × (1 − automated {au})) × (1 + retest {rt}) × environment {env}.
trace.data: Data platform: {f} feeds, {p} pipelines, {t} tables, {c} mapped columns and {q} DQ rules over {l} load cycles = {h} h.
trace.ai: AI product: {i} intents, {s} knowledge sources, {o} OCR document types and {g} guardrail categories, {r} evaluation runs = {h} h of QE time, plus {m} h of SME labelling.
trace.pt: Performance testing: {n} scenarios, {r} runs per cycle × {c} cycles = {h} h.
trace.total: All hours, each including {oh} overhead: application + data + AI + performance = {h} h.
trace.capacity: Capacity: one FTE gives {w} weeks × {dw} days × {ph} productive hours = {hpf} h, × blended capacity {bl} for the team mix = {per} h.
trace.fte: FTE: {h} h ÷ {per} h = {f} FTE, shown as a range of {lo} – {hi} (±{b}%).

steps.0: Pick the mode. No FSD yet: use Rough scope. FSD available: use Detailed scope. Both are always calculated, so the cards and the gap table compare them.
steps.1: Rough scope. List the features or epics. For each, choose the type (Application, Data platform or AI product), T-shirt size and complexity, and tick Perf-critical when it must meet performance targets. Tick the channels in scope and set roles, languages and variants.
steps.2: Detailed scope. Work through the nine numbered sections: application drivers, fields and API payloads, roles and rules, channels, data platform, AI product and performance testing. Leave a section at 0 when the change has no such requirements. Each header shows what the section adds up to; Derived drivers shows how every calculated row is built, and the Complexity guide explains Simple, Medium and Complex.
steps.3: Window, team and environment. SIT weeks, team mix, environment availability, regression automation, AI-assisted test design, AI evaluation runs and SMEs for labelling. Read the Calendar check there: batch windows, labelling lead time or performance environment slots can limit the plan more than FTE.
steps.4: Shift-left evidence. Enter gate results from the delivery team's pipelines: backend, frontend and mobile L1 tests, data pipeline and contract tests, AI evaluation in CI and reused golden sets, performance smoke tests, APM and reused scripts. Use expected values for a Biz Case and actual values before SIT starts.
steps.5: Read the result. The four cards show rough and detailed FTE as ranges, the gap between them and how many assumptions are still uncalibrated. The total combines SIT, data, AI and performance testing. Never quote the single figure without its range.
steps.6: Export. Copy the QBR summary for the deck and export the profile JSON with the project, so the estimate can be reproduced and calibrated later.

0.0: API endpoints, request and response fields
0.1: OpenAPI spec or API design document
0.2: Count unique DTO fields once; classify endpoints with the Complexity guide

1.2: Use Fields by type when the FSD lists field types; it replaces the typical mix

2.2: Each external system or queue is one integration; a core-banking interface with test windows is Complex

3.2: Field-level checks are not rules; count conditions with their own thresholds or outcomes

4.2: Count each state machine once; approval workflows are those with maker-checker steps

5.2: Protected actions exclude workflow transitions, which are added automatically

6.1: Batch schedule, interface specs, event catalogue
6.2: One row per job, file interface or topic

7.2: Tick only the platforms released in this scope

8.1: Source-to-target mapping spec, data model, DQ catalogue, access matrix
8.2: Count mapped columns from the mapping spec; secured datasets are those with row, column or masking rules

9.1: Conversation design or intent list, knowledge base inventory, document samples list, agent tool list
9.2: Count intents and OCR document types by complexity; golden sets and samples must be synthetic

10.1: Non-functional requirements, production volumes and APM data, batch SLAs
10.2: One scenario per business journey, API, batch job or AI call that has a performance target

11.1: Jenkins: PIT, JaCoCo, constraint coverage, Vitest, Stryker, XCTest, Espresso, dbt / Great Expectations, k6 / Gatling reports
11.2: Ask the tech lead for the gate dashboard; use expected gate values when planning ahead

12.1: Environment plan, core-banking test calendar, performance environment schedule
12.2: If SIT depends on shared core-banking windows, choose that option even if other systems are dedicated

items.0: Range, not a point. Rough is ±40% and detailed ±15% by default; the cone of uncertainty suggests wider bands early on. Quote the range in a Biz Case and the mid value only with the range beside it.
items.1: Gap table. Shows which drivers explain the difference between rough and detailed, including data, AI and performance rows. A big gap on one driver usually means the T-shirt proxies need calibrating for your product.
items.2: Sensitivity. The top rows move the estimate most, so calibrate those assumptions first.
items.3: Shift-left credit. The difference between "No gates" and "All gates met" is the cost of not shifting left: a Biz Case argument for the L1 gates.
items.4: Calendar check. When batch windows, SME labelling or performance environment slots do not fit the window, adding FTE will not help; start earlier or extend the window.
items.5: Governance. The FTE and timeline are planning figures. Confirm them with the accountable delivery owner before they go into a commitment.

calibrate.title: Calibration routine after each SIT cycle

items.0: Count the SIT cases actually run per driver and compare them with the derived rows. Adjust cases per driver until the model lands within range.
items.1: Measure minutes per case from the test management tool, separately for functional, validation and mobile cases.
items.2: Take the retest rate from the defect tool: retests ÷ cases run.
items.3: Take productive hours per day from timesheets.
items.4: Count request and response fields in one OpenAPI spec to calibrate the per-endpoint field defaults.
items.5: Data platform: time one load cycle end to end, including data preparation and environment refresh.
items.6: AI product: time the labelling of 50 samples and one evaluation run with human review.
items.7: Performance testing: time one script build per complexity and one full test-and-tune cycle.
items.8: Change the values under Assumptions, name the profile, export it and store it with the project. The next estimate starts from calibrated values.

0.q: Why 6 productive hours per day, not 8?
0.a: Stand-ups, defect triage, reporting and context switching take about 2 hours of every day. Environment waits are counted separately through the environment factor. Measure it from timesheets and change it under Capacity.

1.q: How does Simple / Medium / Complex change the number?
1.a: It sets both the cases per item and the execution minutes per case (10 / 20 / 40), so one complex API costs roughly 7–8 times a simple one. The Complexity guide (section 9 of the Detailed scope tab) explains how to classify each driver.

2.q: How many validation cases if the gate is missed?
2.a: Every field is tested with the full field-type matrix, about 12 cases per field per layer for a typical mix. At 50–99% coverage half of them come back into SIT. The derived rows show the exact calculation for the current evidence.

3.q: Why is backend validation not covered by the frontend?
3.a: Anyone can call the API directly and skip the UI, and API request fields include fields no screen shows. Backend validation uses the API request fields plus API-only cases such as unknown fields and oversized payloads.

4.q: Why does mutation testing not count as SIT work?
4.a: It is automated and owned by the delivery team. It only decides how much logic testing SIT must repeat: below the gate, business-rule cases and the retest rate go up.

5.q: Why are iOS and Android not a full copy of the web cases?
5.a: Mobile channels re-run a share of the web screen and journey cases (60% by default for native apps), add mobile-only cases such as interrupts and offline, and multiply by the device matrix. A full copy would overstate the effort.

6.q: How are data platforms and AI products estimated?
6.a: Mark the features as Data platform or AI product in Rough scope, and fill the Data platform and AI product sections in Detailed scope. Data platforms are sized by feeds, pipelines, tables, mapped columns, data quality rules and reports, with load cycles bound to batch windows. AI products are sized by labelled evaluation samples, human review per evaluation run and analysis, because their outputs are not deterministic. The calendar check warns when batch windows or labelling lead time, not FTE, limit the plan.

7.a: Mark features as performance-critical in Rough scope, or list performance scenarios in section 7 of Detailed scope. Effort comes from scripting each scenario, the workload model, test data at volume, environment and monitoring, runs per test type and test-and-tune cycles, analysis and reporting. It is added to the combined QE total.

8.a: Not yet. Every default is a heuristic and is labelled uncalibrated until your team replaces it with a measured value. The Standards and rationale section explains where each one comes from.

guide.workedExample: Worked example: how the current detailed estimate is built

method.title: How the estimate is calculated
method.formula:
APPLICATION
cases   = Σ counted driver × cases per driver (by complexity)
        + business rules: critical in full, standard credited by rule unit tests, × mutation × variants
        + workflows: transitions × (1 + invalid share)
        + roles: (protected actions + role-gated transitions) × roles × allow/deny × sampling, + segregation of duties
        + frontend validation (screen fields × field-type matrix) + backend validation (API request fields × matrix + API-only cases)
        + mapping (response and payload fields × checks), each after shift-left credit
        + second web stack and languages (share of screen and journey cases)
        + mobile: web journeys × share + (web screens × share + screens × mobile-only cases) × device matrix + release cases, × 1.3 execution
        + accessibility: screens × cases × channels
hours   = Σ cases × [ design min + exec min × (cycles + regression × (1 − automated)) × (1 + retest) × environment ] ÷ 60

DATA PLATFORM
cases   = feeds × cases per feed (after data contract credit) + pipelines × cases + tables × cases + SCD dimensions × extra cases
        + mapped columns × checks + DQ rules × cases (both after pipeline-test credit) + reports × cases
        + secured datasets × access roles × allow/deny × sampling
hours   = Σ data tests × [ design min + exec min × load cycles × (1 + retest) × environment ] ÷ 60
        + reports at application rates + feeds × preparation hours × load cycles

AI PRODUCT
samples = intents × utterances × languages + knowledge sources × questions × languages
        + OCR document types × samples + guardrail categories × adversarial prompts
hours   = samples × [ labelling min × (1 − reused) × QE share + evaluation runs × review share × review min ] ÷ 60
        + (agent tools + human-in-the-loop steps) as cases at application rates + evaluation runs × analysis hours
SME     = samples × labelling min × (1 − reused) × (1 − QE share)  → calendar check, not QE FTE

PERFORMANCE TESTING
hours   = scenarios × scripting h × (1 − reused) + workload model + test data at volume
        + environment and monitoring (+ mobile device checks)
        + Σ test types (runs × hours per run) × test-and-tune cycles × (1 + analysis share) + report

ALL PROFILES
FTE     = (application + data + AI + performance hours) × (1 + overhead) ÷ ( weeks × days per week × productive hours × blended capacity )
range   = FTE × (1 ± band)        band: rough ±40% · detailed ±15%

steps.0: Rough and detailed use the same formula. Rough fills the driver counts from feature size proxies and uses the longer design time per case, because there is no FSD to design from.
steps.1: Field validation is credited by coverage. At 100% the team proved it in L1/L2, so SIT runs one sample per screen (frontend) or per API (backend). At 50–99% half the field-type matrix comes back into SIT; below 50% all of it does, about 12 cases per field per layer for a typical mix. Backend validation is not covered by the frontend: it uses the API request fields, which include fields no screen shows, plus API-only cases such as unknown fields and oversized payloads. Mapping is sized by response and payload fields. Validation and mapping cases use their own lighter effort rates and one full pass, because they are templated and data-driven.
steps.2: A mutation score below the gate means logic defects reach SIT. Business-rule cases go up and the retest rate rises.
steps.3: Roles use a role × guarded-action matrix with risk-based sampling, never roles × every case. Guarded actions are the protected actions outside workflows plus the role-gated workflow transitions. Each approval workflow adds segregation-of-duties cases.
steps.4: Business rules split into critical and standard. Critical rules always run the full decision table in SIT. Standard rules are credited by business rule unit tests: one wiring case each when proven, half the table at 50–99%, the full table below 50%. Rules that vary by product, segment or currency are sampled pairwise.
steps.5: A second web stack or an extra language adds a sampled share of screen and journey cases. Native iOS and Android channels re-run a share of the web cases, add mobile-only cases, multiply by the device and OS matrix and add release cases; they run 1.3× slower. Accessibility adds WCAG cases per screen and channel. Environment availability stretches execution time. Regression automation shrinks only the regression pass; building and maintaining that automation is not counted here.
steps.6: Data platforms are sized by feeds, pipelines, tables, mapped columns, data quality rules and reports. Data tests are cheap SQL comparisons, but each load cycle is bound to a batch window, so the calendar check compares load cycles with the SIT window. Pipeline tests (dbt, Great Expectations) and data contract tests reduce what SIT repeats.
steps.7: AI products are not sized as pass/fail cases, because their outputs are not deterministic. They are sized by labelled evaluation samples, a human review of part of the outputs on every evaluation run, and analysis time. Labelling shared with business SMEs is shown in the calendar check, not in QE FTE.
steps.8: Performance testing is sized by scripted scenarios, runs per test type and test-and-tune cycles, plus workload modelling, test data at volume, environment and monitoring, analysis and reporting. It is part of the combined QE total. Performance smoke tests in CI, APM / OpenTelemetry and reused scripts reduce the effort.
steps.9: Mutation testing itself is never counted as SIT work. It is automated and owned by the delivery team; it only changes how much SIT has to repeat.

standards.title: Standards and rationale
standards.intro: No global standard prescribes numbers such as cases per API or minutes per case. Standards define the methods; the numbers come from your own history. This model follows recognised methods and labels every number as a heuristic until a team calibrates it.

headings.0: Techniques and references the model relies on
headings.2: Ranges against the cone of uncertainty
headings.3: How to calibrate, using the ISTQB techniques
headings.4: Wording for a Biz Case or QBR

0.2: Equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision table testing, state transition testing and combinatorial techniques. The per-driver defaults approximate the smallest case set these techniques produce.

1.2: Four recognised methods: ratio-based, extrapolation, Wideband Delphi and three-point. This model is ratio-based; the other three are how you calibrate it.

2.2: Size × environment factor × productivity factor, plus an allowance for planning and control (about 10%). The capacity factors (0.7–1.2×) and the 15% overhead follow the same shape.

3.2: Estimate error narrows by stage: 0.25×–4× at initial concept, 0.5×–2× at approved product definition, 0.67×–1.5× at requirements complete.

4.1: NIST combinatorial testing research, Kuhn et al. 5
4.2: Most failures are triggered by one or two interacting factors, which justifies sampling the role × action matrix. NIST also warns that pairs alone are not always enough.

5.2: Test cases ≈ function points<sup>1.2</sup>. Needs an IFPUG or COSMIC function point count. Seen in secondary sources; check the original text before citing.

6.2: Time behaviour, resource use and capacity as quality characteristics; load, stress, soak, spike and scalability test types and the workload model.

7.2: Mapped columns, row-count reconciliation per table and data quality rules drive the data estimate; no ISO standard prescribes the numbers.

8.2: The test oracle problem: AI outputs are evaluated against labelled datasets and thresholds rather than single expected results.

9.1: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 8, NIST AI 600-1 generative AI profile 9
9.2: Guardrail categories to red-team, such as prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure and system prompt leakage.

0.derivation: Happy path, two invalid classes, one auth case, one or two boundary or error cases

2.derivation: Happy path, negative, timeout, retry, data mismatch, reconciliation

3.derivation: Average branches in a decision table

4.value: Field validation 3–18 cases per field and layer, by field type (≈12 for a typical mix)
4.derivation: Null, empty, space, min, max, boundary, type, format, enum, duplicate, special, unicode and injection, per the field validation matrix (equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis)

5.value: Validation effort: 2 min design, 3 min UI or 2 min API execution, one full pass
5.derivation: Cases are templated per field type and run data-driven, then only failures are retested

6.derivation: Happy path, empty input, partial failure and restart, cut-off timing, rejects and duplicates, reconciliation

7.derivation: Publish and consume, ordering, duplicate delivery, poison message and dead-letter queue, replay

8.derivation: One case per valid transition plus invalid transitions (state transition testing, ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-4)

9.derivation: Submit, approve, reject and release are usually permission-checked, so they join the role × action matrix

10.derivation: The maker cannot approve their own request; a second user with the checker role can

11.value: 30% critical rules, 1 wiring case per proven standard rule
11.derivation: Regulatory and money-moving rules are always tested in full; other rules need one end-to-end case when L1 proves the logic

12.derivation: Rules that differ by product, segment or currency, sampled pairwise instead of every combination

13.value: Channel shares: second web stack 40%, iOS 60%, Android 60%; extra language 20%
13.derivation: Native apps re-run a sampled share of the web screen and journey cases, not a full copy; a second web stack shares most logic

14.derivation: Interrupts (call, notification), background and foreground, offline and poor network, rotation, back navigation, permission prompts, biometrics or PIN, deep links

15.value: 3 device and OS combinations, +20% per extra combination; 30% of mobile cases need new design
15.derivation: Pairwise sample of devices and OS versions rather than every combination (NIST interaction rule)

16.value: 6 release cases per mobile platform, mobile execution 1.3×
16.derivation: Install, upgrade with existing data, uninstall and store build acceptance; device setup and app rebuilds slow manual runs

17.value: Accessibility 2 cases per screen per channel
17.derivation: Screen reader labels and keyboard or focus order, as WCAG 2.x requires; often regulatory for banking

18.derivation: Shaped on the TPA environment factor: waits for shared downstream systems and core-banking test windows

19.derivation: Reduces the manual regression pass only; automation build and maintenance are outside this estimate

20.derivation: Pairwise-style reduction; use the full matrix for high-risk actions such as approvals and payments

22.value: Mapping: 1 check per response or payload field, plus a format check for 40% of fields
22.derivation: Round trip of every value, plus money, date and enum formats; null handling is part of the round trip

23.value: Request fields 5 / 10 / 20, response fields 8 / 15 / 30 per endpoint, 30% DTO reuse, 12 fields per event
23.derivation: Used only when the FSD or OpenAPI spec gives no count; shared DTOs are counted once

24.derivation: Unknown or extra field (mass assignment), wrong content type, oversized payload, missing body; the UI never sends these (OWASP API Security Top 10)

25.derivation: Mirrors common coverage gates; UI logic defects otherwise surface as screen defects in SIT

26.derivation: Stryker's default low threshold; weak frontend tests let logic defects through

29.derivation: Common focus-factor convention (75% of an 8-hour day): the rest goes to stand-ups, defect triage, reporting and context switching; environment waits are covered by the environment factor. Easy to measure from timesheets

30.value: AI-assisted test design: 0% / 20% / 40% less design time
30.derivation: Applies to designing cases and synthetic test data only, not to execution or environment waits; off by default until a pilot measures it

31.value: Data: 3 / 4 / 6 per feed, 4 / 6 / 9 per pipeline, 2 / 3 / 4 per table, 1.5 per mapped column, 2 per DQ rule
31.derivation: Completeness, schema drift, load modes, restart, reconciliation, source-to-target value checks

32.value: Data effort: 10 min design, 5 min per load cycle, 3 cycles, 2 h data preparation per feed per cycle
32.derivation: Data tests are SQL comparisons, cheap to run but bound to batch windows and data refreshes

33.value: AI: 20 / 35 / 50 utterances per intent, 15 questions per source, 50 / 100 / 200 OCR samples, 40 prompts per guardrail
33.derivation: Golden-set sizes large enough to measure accuracy per intent or document type with useful confidence

34.value: AI effort: 2–6 min labelling per sample, 20% (automated) or 60% human review per run, 6 h analysis per run, 50% of labelling by QE
34.derivation: Labelling the golden set is the main cost; automated evaluation reduces review but a person still checks a sample

35.value: Performance: 4 / 8 / 16 h scripting per scenario, 3 test-and-tune cycles, analysis 50% of execution
35.derivation: Load 3 × 4 h, stress 2 × 4 h, soak 1 × 12 h, spike 1 × 2 h per cycle; 24 h environment and monitoring setup without APM, 8 h with it

36.derivation: Shaped on TPA environment and productivity factors

calibrate.0: Ratio-based: run this model on one or two completed projects and compare it with their actual cases and hours. Adjust cases per driver until it lands within range.
calibrate.1: Extrapolation: after the first SIT cycle, replace execution minutes per case, retest rate and productive hours with what the team measured.
calibrate.2: Three-point: where there is no data yet, ask three senior testers for optimistic (a), most likely (m) and pessimistic (b) minutes per case and use E = (a + 4m + b) ÷ 6.
calibrate.3: Wideband Delphi: agree cases per driver across QE leads in short rounds, then export the result as the shared calibration profile.

standards.wording: The case-count method follows ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-4 test design techniques and ISTQB ratio-based estimation. The effort structure is modelled on TMap Test Point Analysis, and the ranges follow the cone of uncertainty. The numeric defaults are uncalibrated heuristics and will be replaced with actuals after the first SIT cycle.

refs.1: ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level 4.0, section 5.1.4 Estimation techniques. <a1>Study notes</a1> · <a2>CQI | IRCA overview</a2>
refs.2: TMap, Test Point Analysis. <a1>tmap.net</a1> · <a2>Estimation based on test object size</a2>
refs.3: Construx (McConnell), The Cone of Uncertainty. <a1>White paper (PDF)</a1>. The original ranges came from expert judgment, not measured data.
refs.4: NIST, Interactions involved in software failures. <a1>csrc.nist.gov</a1> · <a2>FAQ</a2>
refs.5: Capers Jones sizing rules of thumb, as summarised in University of Zurich seminar slides (PDF). Original: Jones, Applied Software Measurement.
refs.6: ISO/IEC TR 29119-11:2020, Software and systems engineering — Software testing — Part 11: Guidelines on the testing of AI-based systems. <a1>iso.org</a1>
refs.8: NIST AI 600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (July 2024). <a1>NIST (PDF)</a1>
